vignette:
For forty years, Fatima had walked the tiers of the state penitentiary with an unshakeable calm. At sixty-eight, she was a respected senior officer, her quiet authority a steadying presence on the block. That changed seven months ago, on a Tuesday that began like any other. The usual cacophony of the C-Block-shouted conversations, clanging doors, the blare of televisions-died down with an unnatural suddenness. In the strange, pressing silence that followed, Fatima felt a prickle of unease. Before she could turn, an inmate, recently transferred and flagged for unpredictable violence, lunged from an unsecured cell. He shoved her younger partner, Daniel, hard against the bars and came at her with a makeshift weapon. Fatima froze for a split second, a moment that felt like an eternity, before her training kicked in. By the time backup arrived, Daniel was on the ground with a broken arm, and Fatima was left with a deep sense of a duty catastrophically failed.

In the weeks that followed, Fatima found that the silence of her own home had become as threatening as the one on the cell block. She came to believe that she had failed Daniel, that a more vigilant officer would have anticipated the attack. This conviction, that she was no longer competent to protect others, became a constant, humming dread. This sense of failure and mistrust bled into a pervasive feeling of threat; if she couldn't keep her own partner safe in a place she knew better than her own home, then danger was truly everywhere. She began having trouble sleeping, her nights spent staring at the ceiling, her body wired and waiting for a threat that never materialized. She felt permanently estranged from her colleagues, as if her failure had marked her as an outsider among the people she once considered family.

This persistent sense of being unsafe, coupled with her profound self-blame, began to dictate her every action. Her body now seemed to operate on its own hair-trigger system; a tray clattering in the prison cafeteria would make her heart pound and her hands clench before her mind even registered the sound. Feeling so physically out of control, so constantly on edge, was for Fatima the most convincing proof she had that she was fundamentally broken, no longer the calm, competent officer she used to be. This physical hyper-arousal drove her to constantly scan her surroundings, her head on a perpetual swivel, checking exits and monitoring the faces of everyone she passed. The belief that she had failed and was now irrevocably different from her peers made being alone with her thoughts unbearable. To escape them, she began filling every moment with noise and people. At home, the television blared from the moment she walked in until she fell into a fitful sleep, and she insisted on hosting family for dinner almost every night, a desperate measure to keep the silence at bay.

These strategies, meant to keep her safe, only tightened the trap. Her constant environmental scanning confirmed her body's belief that threat was imminent, leaving her more exhausted and jumpy than ever. Giving up her role as a training officer for new recruits-a responsibility she told her captain she could no longer handle-cemented her private conviction that she was a failure. Her frantic need for constant socialising, while preventing her from having to confront her thoughts, also reinforced her feeling of being an outsider; she was present in the conversations but never truly part of them, merely using the noise as a shield. The more she engaged in these behaviours, the more she believed that people couldn't be trusted and that she was fundamentally broken, which in turn amplified her feeling of being under constant, inescapable threat.

Fatima's life has now shrunk into a small, loud, and fearful routine. Her husband, a patient man, is growing weary of a home that no longer has a moment of peace. At work, the job she once took immense pride in has become a source of daily terror. She finally sought help after her captain, a man she had known for twenty years, took her aside and told her he was worried, that the woman who had mentored dozens of young officers seemed to have disappeared. Fatima sat in the therapist's office, her hands clasped tightly in her lap, and admitted that her greatest fear was that he was right. She wasn't sure if the capable, confident person she used to be was someone she could ever be again.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not describe how Fatima's general sense of threat reinforces her negative beliefs about herself or the world.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
